output.title: The Cutting of the String
output.prologue: Hesk the Reel sat at the pole with her spindle and counted every knot the islands flew. Then Aun took his knife to the string, because he wanted to know how far the wind went. This is the account she kept, from the first turn of the thread to the last cord hanging in the south. Every lamp in Vel is a line she tallied, and every one cost something. Listen, and count with her.

stops.text: Mother Hesk sat at the pole with her drop spindle, drawing the string out thin and winding it on the whorl so the islands would not drift. The sky lay low and close over the houses, and the smoke went straight up to it. Aun came up the cliff with his knife in his belt and a question in his mouth. Hesk did not look up. She only said, Count the turns before you cut.

Hesk wound every string the islands flew and kept the count of each knot in her two hands. When the knife went through, she did not stop. The sky drifted off with its knots still in it, and she counted them going, one by one, because a count left unfinished is a debt. Her hands were quick. The first total she reached was smaller than the islands had expected.

When Aun cut the string, the sky went off like a sail torn from its mast. Tavo the Gale heard it and laughed so hard the cliffs rang. A gull named Sokul was working the north ledge that morning, riding the updraft with her eye on a fish, and the sky took her wing and her fish together. She screamed once and then said nothing more, and the wind carried her off.

When Aun cut the string, the gulls flew after the sky. They went up past the last of the wind and came home with nothing but cold in their feathers. Ennu the Kite-Wright sat in the wet at the cliff-foot, and the gulls came down in a grey heap, shivering, and would not eat. So Ennu wove one gull from sailcloth and goose-bone, and set it on the rock to keep them company.

When Aun cut the string, a gull was still on it. Ennu had made her that spring from sailcloth and goose bone, and she was the best flier on the cliffs. She hung on the last yard of the line, beating against the pull, and would not let go. Hesk sent word up the line that she was counted. Tesmal stays, and so a thread still runs from the Reel to one bird.

Kael the Netter cast his net off the north cliffs for a star that had come down too low. He had waited all his life for a catch. The net came up heavy and dripping, and the star was gone; in its place was a gull, wet and furious, with a bit of the star's light still caught in one feather. Kael did not know whether to be glad. He let the gull go, and it flew back to the cliff.

Storm-petrels nest in the cracks of the north cliff, where no fox can reach, and their chicks are dark and quiet. Old Hesk the Reel counted them every autumn with a knot for each one. This autumn she had to tie a knot for every bird that did not come back to the ledge. She tied them slowly. The cord grew heavy at her fingers, and the wind, which had nothing to carry, rubbed it with its thumb.

When Aun cut the string, the rope that held the sky came apart in his hands, and the sky went up with its ends frayed. Mother Hesk sent the Gulls down to say so. They came over the cliffs in a long grey line, crying the news from house to house, and every house heard it before the kettle boiled.

In the year of the great thaw, Tavo the Gale laughed and the valleys ran full. Brown water came down off the hills and sank the lower boats at their moorings, and the men who had gone up the hill for goats came down to find the bay full of masts. Nobody counted the boats that year. Hesk counted them later, from the pole, and the number was not small.

When Aun cut the string, the sky went up so fast that the voyagers of the Leeward boats lost their bottom. The men let out line after line, and each ran out into nothing. Nobody knew how deep the Upper Sea went. Hesk tallied every fathom they gave her, and then she stopped tallying, because the last line had no end.

Mesket's husband took his boat out past the Leeward rocks in the autumn gales, and the sea kept the boat and the man. Mesket did not weep where the children could see. She set the lamp in the window and trimmed the wick, and each night she trimmed it a little less, to keep the oil for the next. The lamp burns low now, and she counts the oil against the nights.

When Aun cut the string he did not know that a sky has weight. Tavo the Gale came in under the drift and lifted the first boats clean off the water, the way a gust lifts a hat. They went up with their sails full and their crews holding the thwarts, and then the wind let go of them all at once, and the lanterns of the lost boats were the last things Hesk counted that day.

When Aun cut the string, the first things to drift past the last lamp were the drowned, and none of them knew the way. A boatman of the Upper Sea, grey-bearded and patient, came out to the edge of the light with his oar across his knees. He called them one by one and took no fare. Those he could reach he rowed ahead, and the rest he let drift past, still calling.

Tavo the Gale was once out over the Windward cliffs in a fury, because a kite-line had been stiff with salt and would not bend for him. He bit it through, and the line parted with a crack like a gull's wing. The cut end whipped away into the dark. That was the second cutting, and nobody thanked him for it.

When Aun cut the string, the sky went up but did not come all the way free. A short length of cord stayed knotted to his hand, and it still hangs in the Unflown, where the wind does not come back. Hesk counted that too. It is the one line still tied to anything, and the people say that whoever ties to its end and waits for a still day may be drawn back up toward the islands.
